opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by "abstraction." In our own work, we've tried to make this precise with simple generative models of data that have a hierarchical, compositional structure: features are built from sub-features, which are built from sub-sub-features, and so on, a bit like a grammar. In that setting you can say quite concretely what it means for a network to have learned an abstraction. A hidden representation becomes invariant to the exact low-level realization of something, the specific synonyms if you like, while still encoding the higher-level variable that matters for the task. And you can then ask how many examples you need before that invariance emerges. Roughly, it happens when there are enough data for the correlations between the low-level tokens and the high-level variable to be detectable above sampling noise. That gives you a sample complexity, and it also explains why depth helps: you build the abstraction level by level.

But that's learning the abstraction. Using it is a different question, and that's where I think most of the open problems are.

The first one is composition. Once a network has learned that a certain set of patches or tokens are "equivalent" at some level, can it recombine those abstract variables in ways it has never seen? In a sense that's the whole point of having an abstraction. If you only use it to interpolate within the training distribution, you haven't gained much. We see hints of this in diffusion models: if you add noise and denoise, at intermediate noise levels the low-level details change while the high-level class is preserved, and there's a sharp, phase-transition-like point where the high-level structure suddenly changes. That suggests the model represents the hierarchy in a way it can manipulate. But going from "the representation reflects the hierarchy" to "the model can reliably reason with it" is not at all understood.

The second issue is that real data are not a clean tree. In language or images you have context-dependence, long-range correlations, ambiguity, many overlapping hierarchies. So an open question is which aspects of our simple models are robust. Is the scaling of sample complexity with depth and vocabulary size something you actually see in large language models? There are some encouraging signs, for example the way the effective context a model uses grows with the training set size, but it's far from settled.

Third, and I think this matters a lot for practice, is the relationship between abstraction and data efficiency. Humans seem to learn abstractions from remarkably few examples, partly because we reuse them across tasks. Current networks largely learn them from scratch, with enormous datasets. If we understood which abstractions are learned at which point in training, and how they could be transferred or reused, that might lead to much more efficient learning, and perhaps to architectures that are biased toward the right kind of compositionality from the start.

Finally there's the interpretability side. If abstractions really are invariances in latent space, we should be able to detect them, measure them, and maybe even intervene on them. But measuring the right invariance requires knowing what the latent variables are, and in real data we generally don't. So there's a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem. Synthetic models help because you know the ground truth, but the challenge is to build bridges to natural data without fooling ourselves.

So to summarize: I think we're starting to understand when and why abstractions emerge. How they are used, for composition, for reasoning, for transfer, is still largely open, and I find that a very exciting place to be.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that we don't really understand yet what these abstractions are. We have evidence, from the hierarchical models we and others have studied, that deep networks learn a compositional structure: low-level features get grouped into higher-level ones, and the network discovers synonyms, in the sense that different combinations of low-level inputs that play the same role in the data get mapped to the same latent variable. That's what gives you the dramatic gain in sample complexity, because once you have collapsed those synonyms you don't need to see every combination anymore. But that's a picture from very idealized generative models. Whether it is really what is going on in a large language model or a diffusion model trained on natural images, we only have indirect evidence.

So the open questions, as I see them, are of a few kinds.

The first is about transfer. If the network has built a latent variable that represents, say, a verb phrase or the notion of an object, can that variable actually be reused in a context the network hasn't seen? The theory tells you that representing the latent is useful for predicting within the training distribution. It says much less about whether the variable is accessible and composable in a new task. Learning a representation and being able to manipulate it are not the same thing, and I think a lot of the excitement around in-context learning or reasoning is really a question about the second.

The second is what controls which abstractions get learned. In our hierarchical models the curriculum is set by statistics: you learn the correlations that are strongest first, and the size of the training set determines how deep in the hierarchy you can go. That suggests the abstractions you get are determined by the data, not by anything we would recognize as what matters semantically. If the correlation structure of the data doesn't single out a concept, the network won't build it, even if the concept would be useful downstream. So a very practical open question is how you shape the data, or the objective, so that the latents you want actually emerge, and whether there is a way to see that from the learning curve rather than by probing afterwards.

The third, and the one I find the most interesting physically, is the question of hierarchy versus something flatter. The models we can solve are trees. Real data is not a tree: the same latent appears in many places, there are long-range dependencies, there are structures that are closer to graphs. We don't yet know how the sample complexity scales in that setting, or whether the mechanism of collapsing synonyms still carries most of the explanatory weight. My intuition is that it does, but intuition is cheap here.

And finally there is the question of how much of this is stable. When you fine-tune, or when you continue training on new data, do these abstractions survive, do they get refined, or do they get destroyed and rebuilt? There is almost no theory on that, and it matters a lot if you want to put the representations to use rather than just admire them.

So in short, we are at the stage where we can say why learning compositional latents is possible and why it beats the curse of dimensionality. Going from that to a theory of how those latents can be exploited, transferred, and controlled is, I think, the real frontier.

astra-6.text:
I think one open question is what it means to have learned an abstraction. You may have a latent representation in which some useful variable is easy to identify, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the system can use it to solve a new problem.

For example, can it take something learned in one setting and use it in another, where the superficial details are different? Can it combine two things it has learned separately? And how much additional data does that require? These are ways to make the question more precise.

There is also a distinction between having information in a representation and being able to access it through learning. If I can extract a variable with a carefully trained probe, that tells me something about the representation. But it doesn’t yet explain whether the system itself will discover how to use that variable efficiently. I think understanding that connection—between the structure of representations and the learning dynamics of a downstream task—is a very interesting open problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the big questions is: even if you have learned a useful representation, how do you know which aspects of it you should use for a new task? You might have variables that capture the structure of the world, but that doesn’t automatically tell you how to reason with them or how to act.

And then there is the question of composition. If you learn an abstraction in one setting, can you combine it with another abstraction and use it in a situation you have never encountered? That seems to be a very important aspect of intelligence. We don’t just recognize things; we reuse what we know under different circumstances.

So I would distinguish learning a representation from learning the operations you can perform on that representation. How those two things should be learned together, and what makes the resulting abstractions transferable, I think are still very open questions.
